newsitem.title: USA: Ethics panel evenly split again for Gingrich case.
newsitem.headline: Ethics panel evenly split again for Gingrich case.

text.p: A Republican member of the House ethics committee said Wednesday he has stepped aside from the Gingrich case to restore the panel's even party split following the departure of Democrat Jim McDermott in a controversy over a leaked tape.
"I will not participate in any further actions of the Committee on Standards of Official Conduct relative to the speaker's case," Representative David Hobson of Ohio said.

McDermott stepped aside Tuesday, one day after a Florida couple said they handed him a tape of a Dec. 21 conference phone call involving House Speaker Newt Gingrich and his top lieutenants. Leaks of the tape were published two days later.
The couple told a news conference they picked up the cellular phone call on a police scanner while driving near Jacksonville, Florida, and taped it.

Until McDermott stepped down the ethics panel was split 5-5 between Republicans and Democrats. Hobson's departure means a 4-4 panel will decide on the appropriate punishment to recommend for Gingrich's admitted ethics violations.

The full House is to vote on the penalty -- expected to be a reprimand -- next Tuesday. A report on the case by special counsel James Cole was expected to be released Thursday, followed by a public hearing.

Hobson said in a statement that McDermott's "apparent offer" to step aside from the committee would upset the party balance, "which is essential to the ethics process." The Washington state Democrat had made his decision to leave conditional on action to keep the panel balanced politically.

Hobson has reached the six-year limit for ethics committee service and would normally have been replaced at the start of the new Congress, but he said he had reluctantly agreed to stay on the panel until it had dealt with the Gingrich case.
He said he now believed his decision to step aside "will help heal the divisions in the House and allow it to proceed with the important business of the American people."

Recent developments in the last phases of the Gingrich investigation have soured what had been expected to be a relatively harmonious start to the new Congress and a cooperative relationship with President Clinton.
Clinton, asked Wednesday for his view of the "political warfare" over the case, said: "I want it to be over."

He added: "The American people have given us larger responsibilities. I think in general, at least in my experience in my brief time here the last four years, way too much time and energy and effort is spent on all these things, leaving too little time and emotional energy for the work of the people."
Clinton said Gingrich "should do whatever is appropriate and we should get on with it, put it behind us and go on with the business of the country."

McDermott charged Tuesday that ethics committee Republicans under chairwoman Nancy Johnson of Connecticut had "delayed, stonewalled, or otherwise obstructed sensible efforts to get at the whole truth."

"I can no longer participate in this charade while the present controversy continues," he said. He made no direct mention of the leaked tapes but Republicans have said if he was reponsible for the leak he should resign from Congress.

FBI Director Louis Freeh announced Tuesday he had ordered an immediate investigation into "a possible illegal telephone interception and the subsequent dissemination of the contents of the telephone call."
